title: The Wonderful Adventures of Nils
author: Selma Lagerlöf
short_summary: Nils Holgersson likes eating, sleeping and tormenting the animals on his family's farm — until he catches a tomte in a net, refuses its offer of a gold coin and is shrunk to the size of a thumb. When the farm's white gander takes off after a flock of wild geese, Nils grabs his neck and goes with him, and spends a year crossing the whole length of Sweden on the back of a goose, learning the country and slowly becoming somebody worth turning back.
extended_summary:
The book began as a commission: in 1902 the National Teachers Association asked Selma Lagerlöf to write a geography reader for Swedish schools. What she produced is a fairy tale in which the geography is the journey — a boy carried the length of the country, province by province, by a flock of migrating geese.

Nils is a boy whose chief pleasures are eating, sleeping and making mischief, particularly at the expense of the farm animals. One day he catches a tomte in a net. The tomte offers him a gold coin to be released; Nils refuses, and is shrunk to the size of the tomte himself, able to understand every animal on the farm — all of whom remember exactly how he has treated them.

When the farm's white gander, Martin, tries to fly off with the wild geese, Nils seizes his neck and is carried into the air. The flock is led by Akka from Kebnekaise, an old grey goose who has no reason to trust a human; Smirre the fox follows them across the country. Over the months Nils learns that he can be turned back if he can show that he has changed — and by then he has stopped being the boy who tied the animals' tails together.

questions.prompt: This book was not simply invented for fun — it was commissioned. What was it originally written to be?

options: A geography reader for Swedish schoolchildren
A Christmas story for a newspaper competition
A guidebook for travellers visiting Sweden
A collection of folk tales about farm animals

questions.explanation: The National Teachers Association asked Lagerlöf for a school geography book, and she wrote a boy onto the back of a goose so that the whole country could be seen from above. That is why the journey is so long and so orderly: the route is the syllabus.

questions.prompt: Nils catches a tomte in a net. What happens next?

options: He refuses a gold coin, and is shrunk to a tomte's size
He asks for three wishes, and the last one goes wrong
He lets it go, and it rewards him with a magic feather
He sells it at the market, and is cursed by its family

questions.explanation: The tomte offers him a coin for its freedom, and Nils — being the kind of boy he is at that point — wants more. The punishment is exactly fitted to the crime: the boy who tormented small creatures is made into one.

questions.prompt: When the wild geese fly over the farm, the white farmyard gander tries to go with them. His name is ___.
questions.explanation: He is a tame farm bird who has never flown further than the yard, and the wild geese jeer at him for trying. That he keeps up at all — with a boy on his neck — is the first thing in the book that anybody does out of pure stubbornness.

questions.prompt: Who leads the flock of wild geese that Nils travels with?

options: Akka from Kebnekaise
Smirre from Skåne
Bataki from Uppsala
Gorgo from Lapland

questions.explanation: Akka is an old grey goose named after a mountain in the far north, and she has led the flock for many years. She has no reason at all to accept a human passenger, and most of the first half of the book is Nils earning the right to stay.

questions.prompt: Put the beginning of Nils's story in the order it happens.

items: Nils spends his days eating, sleeping and tormenting the animals
He catches a tomte in a net and refuses its gold coin
He is shrunk, and finds he can understand the animals
The white gander tries to fly off with the wild geese
Nils grabs the gander's neck and is carried into the air
The flock, led by Akka, lets the two of them come along

questions.explanation: Four of these five steps happen in a single morning. Lagerlöf gets her hero off the ground almost immediately — and note the order: Nils can understand the animals *before* he leaves, which means he has to hear what they think of him first.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their part in the story.

right: Shrinks Nils for refusing a fair offer
The farm gander who carries him
The old grey goose who leads the flock
The fox who follows them across the country

questions.explanation: One character punishes him, one carries him, one judges him and one hunts him — and none of them is human. For most of the book Nils is the only person in it, which is precisely the point of his punishment.

questions.prompt: Nils is not the same boy at the end as at the beginning. Sort each detail.

content.groupA: The Nils of the first chapter

options.label: Likes eating and sleeping better than anything
Amuses himself by tormenting the farm animals
Wants more than the tomte's gold coin
Keeps watch at night while the flock sleeps
Is trusted by an old goose who distrusts humans
Learns the name of every province he flies over

questions.explanation: The change is the plot: the tomte's condition is not a task to complete but a person to become. Everything in the right-hand column is something the boy in the left-hand column would have had no interest in whatsoever.

questions.prompt: Why does the story send Nils the whole length of the country instead of keeping him in one place?

options: The book was meant to teach the geography of Sweden
The geese are trying to escape from Smirre the fox
The tomte ordered him to visit every province in turn
Martin is searching for the flock he was hatched in

questions.explanation: Every province gets its landscape, its towns and its stories, because that was the assignment. Lagerlöf's solution — put the reader on a goose — is why a school textbook turned into a book people still read for pleasure a century later.

questions.prompt: The tomte punishes Nils by shrinking him to the size of a thumb and leaving him among animals who remember exactly how he treated them. Was that a fair punishment for a boy who teased farm animals? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both positions can earn full marks. A strong 'fair' answer notices that the punishment fits the crime exactly and that it is the only thing that could have changed him. A strong 'too harsh' answer notices that he loses a year of his life, is nearly eaten several times, and that his parents believe he has vanished. Accept either, argued from the book.

questions.prompt: Lagerlöf used a boy on a goose to teach children the geography of their own country. Imagine the geese carried Nils over the place where you live. Describe one thing he would see from above, and one thing he could only learn by landing.
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer gives two genuinely different kinds of knowledge — the shape of a place from above, and something you can only find out on the ground from the people or animals there. That difference is exactly how Lagerlöf built the book.

questions.prompt: The tomte shrinks Nils so small that he can ride all the way across the country on the back of a ___.
questions.explanation: He is left about the size of the tomte itself — small enough to be carried, small enough to be prey, and small enough that a farm cat becomes a serious danger. The size is the whole engine of the plot.

questions.prompt: What does Nils learn during the journey about how he might become a boy again?

options: He must show that he has changed for the better
He must find the tomte and return the gold coin
He must fly all the way to Lapland and back
He must set free every animal he ever trapped

questions.explanation: Not a quest, not an object to fetch — a change that has to be real. That is why the book takes a year and crosses a country: Lagerlöf needs enough time and enough trouble for the change to be believable.
